idiom_name: immutable Version struct + Vec<(NaiveDate, Version)> with partition_point as-of lookup
implementation_notes: The version role is a struct whose fields are owned values, so a snapshot is a value and publishing is a clone plus insert; the continuity owns a Vec ordered by effective date and the as-of lookup is slice::partition_point, which returns the index of the first version after the query so the version in force is one index back (checked_sub covers the before-the-first case). The standard library has no versioning machinery and there is no shared mutable graph to soften the design, so the continuity/version split is hand-written - which is also why it fits Rust: change is a new value and published values are simply not mutated. chrono::NaiveDate is the conventional effective-date key; the std-only variant uses Unix seconds when a dependency is unwanted.
pitfalls: The snapshot is only as immutable as its fields: clone is shallow, so a Vec/HashMap/Rc field inside Version is shared with the previous version and interior mutability can still rewrite history - keep versions owned and plain.
partition_point requires the slice to be partitioned by the predicate (true run then false run); appending an out-of-order version breaks that invariant and returns a wrong index without any panic.
NaiveDate carries no time zone and no instant: mixing it with NaiveDateTime::now in local time shifts effective dates, so convert once at the boundary and store one representation.
Vec::insert shifts the tail and invalidates references taken earlier in the same function; do not hold &Version across an amendment.

variants.name: Dependency-free history keyed by std::time (Unix seconds)
variants.idiom_name: Vec<(i64, Version)> keyed by seconds since UNIX_EPOCH, partition_point lookup
variants.implementation_notes: When no third-party crates are allowed, the effective date is stored as seconds since UNIX_EPOCH obtained from SystemTime::duration_since, and the history is the same ordered Vec with partition_point or binary_search_by as the lookup - so the structure survives, only the key type changes. The trade-offs show up in the types: std has no calendar arithmetic (no 'first day of next month'), subtracting SystemTime values needs Duration arithmetic, and pre-epoch or platform-specific SystemTime ranges need explicit handling. Choose it for libraries and embedded crates with a no-dependency policy; use chrono when calendar semantics and formatting matter.
pitfalls: SystemTime subtraction must go through duration_since (a Result): the Sub impl panics when the subtrahend is later, so pre-epoch or clock-skew inputs must be handled explicitly.
Unix seconds discard sub-second precision and the platform SystemTime range is not guaranteed to cover all representable i64 values, so far-future scheduled amendments need a documented bound.
Without a calendar type, month- and quarter-based amendment scheduling has to be hand-written and month-end arithmetic is easy to get wrong.
